extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media scholars, journalism students, and news executives
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic guidance and criteria for identifying, understanding, and assessing external pressure, censorship, and self-censorship in news organizations, including sources, mechanisms, vulnerability conditions, and likely outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure = criticism, organized or unorganized protest, as well as threats against journalists, their organizations, and their firms, applied in order to force journalists to change the news (or to omit a story) or to create a chilling effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes both direct attempts to alter news (censorship) and actions intended to induce voluntary pre-emptive changes (chilling effects). Not all criticism counts as pressure (e.g., requests for factual corrections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists generally define censorship as killing or altering a story as a result of external pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the narrow, journalist-centered definition; the chapter contrasts it with broader institutionalized exclusions (see 'broader definition of censorship').

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-censorship is the (conscious) response to anticipated pressure from nonjournalists; it can also be unconscious, where journalists may not be aware they are responding to pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-censorship includes voluntary anticipatory changes to stories, and may be driven by taste considerations, fear of reprisals, or institutional norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader definition of censorship / institutionalized self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: An outside observer can define censorship more broadly to include built-in limits to journalistic autonomy (value exclusion and mechanisms that anticipate and thereby avoid pressure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the broad view, routine selection practices and anticipatory avoidance become forms of institutionalized censorship/self-censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist responses to pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists can react to pressure in three ways: they can fight; they can give in, altering the news to placate the exerters of pressure; or they can anticipate their critics (voluntarily modifying content beforehand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These responses may be covert (built into judgments) or overt (public complaints, concessions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of external pressure — advertisers
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers may demand killing or altering stories they perceive to hurt them or withdraw advertising to produce a chilling effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National evening news and newsmagazines are relatively insulated; hour-long documentaries and local outlets are more vulnerable. Advertisers can complain only ex post facto because they usually lack advance knowledge of story content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of external pressure — corporate parent / firm
rubrics_metrics.description: The firm that owns the news organization can censor uncomplimentary news about itself; programs or magazines will not carry uncomplimentary news about their firm except to publicize the firm's defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate executives may kill or alter stories; such internal pressure is distinct from external pressure but can be transmitted from outside actors through executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of external pressure — affiliated stations
rubrics_metrics.description: Affiliated local station owners can pressure networks because they can refuse to carry network shows, switch networks, or influence network decisions through affiliate associations and meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiliate pressure is often political/conservative and can lead to removal of individual reporters or complaints about coverage perceived to violate local tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of external pressure — government and public officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Public officials frequently exert pressure (complaints to executives, economic threats, investigations) because they are sensitive to negative coverage and can threaten firms via regulatory or economic levers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government pressure can be conveyed directly to executives, by economic threats (contracts, licenses), or by launching investigations; its effectiveness varies with public interest in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of external pressure — audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences can affect the symbolic arena by critical mail, canceling subscriptions, switching stations, or refusing to view content; audience behavior can produce chilling effects focused on taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste considerations may be the major form of self-censorship because audience refusal to view/subscribe directly threatens journalists and firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of successful pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable outcomes of successful pressure include killing or altering stories, dismissals or forced resignations of journalists, sponsors withdrawing support, and long-term avoidance of topics (especially in marginal operations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success is relatively rare at national levels but more common in marginal operations (e.g., documentaries) and local media. Dismissals may not create sustained chilling if colleagues regard the punished journalist as a troublemaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of marginal operations (documentaries, local productions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hour-long network news documentaries and other marginal operations are particularly vulnerable to pressure because of high production costs, sponsor involvement, prescreening, and influential audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prescreened documentaries allow sponsors and affiliates to protest; sponsor reluctance can discourage production; congressional investigations have targeted documentaries (e.g., 'The Selling of the Pentagon', 'Hunger').

rubrics_metrics.name: National vs local susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: National news organizations are less susceptible to advertiser and business pressure than local newspapers and stations; local media are more easily influenced due to social proximity and economic leverage of local advertisers and power holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National firms can usually replace interfering advertisers and are constrained by potential national publicity; local journalists may face near-permanent chilling effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective institutional arrangements — separation of editorial and business
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation between editorial and business departments reduces susceptibility to advertiser pressure because story selection and advertising placement occur independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top producers/editors are informed of advertisers late in the process and may work with business departments to mitigate conflicts (e.g., postponing or relocating commercials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of economic pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic mechanisms include advertisers canceling ads, threats to revoke government contracts, FCC-related license pressures, and recruiting rivals for broadcast licenses to punish networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Networks are vulnerable due to license structures and government leverage; advertisers' cancellations are often temporary and more frequently based on taste or perceived political bias than direct economic harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political strategies and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Political pressure may take the form of complaints to executives, economic threats, or investigations; its success is constrained by factors like widespread public interest and the networks' own influence within regulators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-audience-interest stories (e.g., Watergate) reduce the effectiveness of government pressure; political actors may use indirect routes (allies owning affiliates, friendly corporations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chilling vs heating effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Chilling effects are reduced reporting or anticipatory avoidance due to pressure or threat; heating effects occur when journalists, angered by pressure attempts, increase investigative effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes heating can follow attempts at pressure (e.g., Watergate reporting intensified), so pressure does not always suppress coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of empirical study and identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying external pressure and its outcomes is empirically and definitionaly difficult because surrender is stigmatized, insiders may not disclose influence, and executives may not relay pressures to journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should account for conscious and unconscious self-censorship, the secrecy of decisions, and retrospective uncertainty about motives (e.g., whether departures were pressure-induced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of taste and subcultural audiences in news selection
rubrics_metrics.description: News content and susceptibility to self-censorship are shaped by taste subcultures (class, education); audience enlargement and cultural democratization may push news toward more personally relevant, less upper-middle-class content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste taboos can generate audience-driven self-censorship; changes in audience composition (aging, education) alter demand for analysis vs action and may pressure news form and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for minority viewpoints and pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure that censors marginal operations can weaken expression of minority viewpoints, which are already peripheral in news ecosystems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even rare successful pressures on marginal outlets have outsized consequences for diversity of perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards and defensive practices by journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: When stories might antagonize powerful actors (advertisers, business, government), journalists tend to be more cautious in processing news, ensuring convincing evidence and retaining files/notes to defend accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top producers/editors check for sponsor conflicts and may coordinate with business departments; this carefulness is both a professional norm and a defensive response to potential pressure.
